title: I built a browser-playable demo of Ghost Engine — same event, different history
author: GhoCentric
selftext:
Ghost is a deterministic state engine for persistent game/AI systems.

Instead of making another reddit post explaining my work, I made a small interactive demo you can click through.

It shows:

the exact same betrayal producing different outcomes from different accumulated histories.

one interaction propagating weighted effects to other NPCs.

facts, reports, evidence, and character beliefs remaining separate.

The released Ghost v1.9.1 Python package is actually running inside the browser through Pyodide. The demo itself makes zero LLM calls.

Play it here:

(Link at the top of the post)

Source/PyPI links are at the end of the demo.

I’m interested in whether the concept makes more sense after actually interacting with it than it did from the written explanations.

replies.author: Tiny-Lake5808
replies.body:
Hey, I've seen you around and feel like commenting because there is something authentic behind wanting to create something useful and share it. I spent quite a bit of time looking around your site, and your source code on GitHub, so I could offer something of substance here. I would like to try and take the time to explain why people look at this and see it as slop. I've seen you complain about being "torn apart" because you're using AI. That's not what this is, I promise. I use AI for work, I have nothing against it as a tool.


Your biggest issue is that you're convinced there's a problem to solve with your solution, but it's just not demonstrably there. This is, at its core, what I think makes up "slop" in general. The quality of your code, number of tests, or how visually appealing the frontend is does not change this. I spent way more time than I'd like to admit coming to this conclusion because I wanted this to not be true. Your engine, at its core, is a state machine. I wasn't able to think of a use case that wouldn't be better served by a state machine that was purpose-made instead of integrating with this. For the example cases you've provided, those state machines are also dreadfully simple to write and maintain.


There's a couple key features that your engine puts forward: Putting in the same input generates different outcomes based on previous state, and the outcome is deterministic if replayed. The first one, different outcomes, is an inherent feature of a simple state machine. If I wanted a different outcome from sequential inputs from the state flow, I would just determine that with a variable in the state. The determinism entirely depends on whether or not state transitions depend on floating point math and whether you care about cross machine compatibility, but if you use integers, decimals, seeded random values, etc. then the determinism generally comes free. Then for some reason you claim zero LLM calls as a feature. I have no idea why that's listed, it's weird to read on the front page. That's sloppy.


The website itself does a poor job of conveying what it's useful for, partially because it's quite opinionated in how it works, and also partially because you constructed this website from context within your project. I think this problem of it being opinionated is hard to avoid, because what you're trying to generalize is typically a very opinionated internal implementation. The site uses a mishmash of technical jargon at particular repetitive cadences that makes it honestly exhausting to read. This is what people will mean by "slop". Terms like "interpretation + attention", "salience bridge", "attention/flow", etc on the front page mean absolutely nothing to the viewer, and there are tiring AI -isms that are prevalent everywhere:

 - "Same event. Different history."
 - "Same event. Two different returned states."
 - "Same fresh setup. Same ordered inputs. Run it twice."
 - "Both guards receive the exact same betrayal event. Only their accumulated history is different."
 - "A claim is not the world."
 - "The fact stayed fixed. The belief record changed."
 - "Same fact. Same report. Same evidence. Reproduce the revision."


The example on your website doesn't really prove anything interesting. It's a button you click to change two visible sliders. Then you do it again? And then go through a bunch of similar slideshow presentations that promise something is working but only in a sort of visually interesting way, not mechanically interesting. An actual game would do you much better than that by miles. Anything to show that it's useful for creating interesting mechanics or to save time implementing complex state management. I saw you've changed the example recently, but the "slop" isn't that it doesn't look nice. It's that it's unnecessary.


On a side note, there's pretty much zero non-python support for actually using your engine. That limits your audience considerably. If I wanted to integrate with this using a different language, I would have to reconstruct all of the types that Ghost uses for the interop. That would require reviewing the source code, which means that your audience is also limited to developers who know how to set that up. You will need to somehow convince anyone that might want to use this library that it saves effort comparable to rolling their own internal logic. Even then, your implementation is very opinionated. So whatever project is integrating with it would also have to conform to whatever terminology you've already defined. This is an extra layer that developers will have to work around rather than naturally integrate with, which creates unnecessary friction. It's not as generic as you would like it to be for a general purpose library. 


My recommendation is that you take a step back from focusing on the presentation of this, and actually try to use it to make something. It's extremely difficult to drum up interest for something unproven, and I think trying to integrate this into a project with spatial or temporal concerns will be enlightening.

replies.author: GhoCentric
replies.body:
Hey, I appreciate the time you took to look at my work. 

I spent like 6 hours going through my git and my ideas/Thesis with my AI. 

You're right.. ghost, at its core is simply a state machine that really doesnt do much better compared to whats used today. Its unfortunate that I messed up this hard but thats life. 

I am going to take your advice and step back a bit. Im not going to give up, but I do understand that my git is lazy and unorganized(Even though i really though it was), my code is good but thats just it.....good... Some places are too bloated. The overhead of my engine is massive too. Some files need to be split, my Thesis drifted and my readmes started to contradict themselvess. On top of that, my benchmarks were not as strong as i thought, even with the extra audits. A lot of errors. A lot of issues. 

The website? Yeah, only makes sense to me because its built from my understand, which was a misunderstanding by miles. 

So yeah, you're right and Im commenting this because I think its only fair to spend some time writing up a reply for someone who took the time to really look into my work. 

Again, I appreciate the efforts.
